title: Your first drawing
objective: Draw a mug from observation, keep the first attempt as a baseline, and use one visible relationship to guide a second drawing.

warmup.instructions: Keep one mug and the same viewpoint. Look for 30 seconds without drawing. Make a 2-minute thumbnail. Spend 1 minute comparing its height with its width or checking the handle opening. Make a second 2-minute thumbnail, changing only that relation. Use the final 90 seconds to circle what changed and note one thing that still looks different. Total: 7 minutes.

explanation: Observation is a repeated exchange: look at the mug, make marks, and compare them with what you see. Keep the first drawing as a record of what you noticed; it does not need to be polished.

Choose one visible relationship to check, such as height against width, the tilt of the rim, or the shape inside the handle. Keep the mug and viewpoint steady, then test that one change in a second drawing. Look back at the mug as you draw.

exercise.instructions:
1. Set one mug where you can see its rim, body, and handle. Choose a comfortable viewpoint and keep it for both drawings. (3 min)
2. Look before drawing. Lightly place a recognizable first drawing, describing the large outline, rim, and handle opening. Keep this attempt; do not erase it. (11 min)
3. Compare the drawing with the mug. Choose one mismatch you can point to, such as body width, rim tilt, or handle opening. Write a short note beside the first drawing. (5 min)
4. In a fresh space, draw the mug again from the same view. Focus on the relationship you chose, and keep checking the rest of the mug against life. (12 min)
5. Look between the mug and both drawings. Mark what changed and note one relationship you want to watch in your next drawing. (4 min)

reflection: Which visible relationship did you choose to improve in the second drawing?
What changed between your first and second drawings when you checked the mug?
extension: Draw the same mug from a new viewpoint and ask the same question: which visible relationship will you check first?

teaching.whyItMatters: Keeping a first attempt lets you see what you noticed before correcting anything. One visible comparison gives you a practical next step for the second drawing.
teaching.connections: The two attempts create a look-draw-check cycle that Lessons 2 and 3 will reuse with contour turns and surrounding gaps.

deepDive: Observation has two partners: making marks while looking, and reviewing those marks after looking back at the subject. If you let a broad judgment speak too early, it can interrupt the act of noticing. Keep the first small drawing as a record, then turn the review into a question with a visible answer: Is the body taller than it is wide? Does the rim rise on the same side? Is the handle opening larger or smaller than you first drew? A useful note describes a relationship you can point to on the mug. It is not a score. The note gives your next look a job and lets you compare a change without erasing what you did first. That record makes practice concrete.

Changing one relationship at a time makes the comparison easier to read. Keep the mug in the same place and keep your chair, head, and page still; then a difference between the two sketches is easier to connect to your new observation. Choose a relation with clear endpoints, such as the body's height against its width, the angle of the rim against the page, or the handle opening against the body. Adjust that relation in the second space, then check the entire mug again. The goal is not a polished finish or a perfectly measured object. You are learning to let a visible observation guide a new mark. In another lesson you can use the same routine to compare a shoe contour or a plant's empty gaps, so the method transfers to new subjects.

commonMistakes.mistake: Drawing a familiar mug symbol instead of checking the mug in front of you.
commonMistakes.lookFor: The rim, body, or handle is made even by habit. Compare one of those features with the actual mug before changing the drawing.
